summary:
Punjab has no statute of its own targeting transgender people. A trans visitor to Punjab stands under India's national framework, which the parent record carries.

The national layer binding Punjab includes the Supreme Court's 6 September 2018 judgment in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, which struck down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, held that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, and preserved the provision for non-consensual acts. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender identity, codified by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing.

The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019) is the national statute governing transgender people in Punjab. It was passed by the Lok Sabha on 5 August 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on 26 November 2019, received presidential assent on 5 December 2019, and has been in force since 10 January 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA ruling, it grants transgender people the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people. On 27 January 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality.

Punjab's own signal is social rather than statutory. Pride Amritsar cancelled its 27 April 2025 Rose Garden parade after mounting resistance from Sikh religious organisations including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, with organisers citing religious-group opposition; the Washington Blade reported this on 23 April 2025. Public visibility of LGBT+ life in Amritsar therefore carries a documented risk of organised religiously-framed obstruction, which a visitor planning to attend or appear at Pride events should weigh.
tangentialFactors:
Criticism of the national Act holds that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education, a gap affecting residents more than short-term visitors.

Punjab's religious landscape, where Sikh institutions carry substantial public authority, is the specific local factor behind the Pride Amritsar cancellation. Organised opposition of this kind is not documented against trans people specifically, but it shapes the environment for any visibly gender-nonconforming or LGBT+ person appearing in public events in the state.
localsOnly:
The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 applies in Punjab as national law, granting residents the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without sex reassignment surgery, banning discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing, and creating a National Council for Transgender Persons. Penalties for crimes against transgender people run from six months to two years' imprisonment plus a fine.

Residents of Punjab can rely on the 2014 NALSA recognition of a legal third gender and self-identified gender identity, and on Navtej Singh Johar's holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution. The July 2024 replacement of the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 removed Section 377 from the statute book.

Punjab has no state-level transgender welfare board or Punjab-specific trans statute or institution. The Supreme Court's 27 January 2020 notice on a petition challenging the 2019 Act's constitutionality remains pending as far as this inventory records.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the March 2026 amendment to India's transgender recognition framework, carried in the parent record, has been implemented in Punjab through state-level procedures is unresolved in this inventory; the source claims here predate or do not address that amendment's on-the-ground operation in Punjab.

No Punjab-specific data on police conduct toward trans people, document-checkpoint incidents, conversion-therapy practice, or healthcare access for trans visitors was identified. The inventory contains no Punjab incident of the kind documented elsewhere in India (airport stops, railway police conduct, medical-exam demands at passport offices).

Whether Pride Amritsar has rescheduled or abandoned the parade after the April 2025 cancellation is not sourced.
